title: Prompt engineering best practices for 2026
author: Anthropic
summary: A single page that moves from four everyday prompting habits (say exactly what you want, explain why it matters, be specific, show one example) to advanced moves such as prefilling Claude's reply to force clean JSON, guided and structured chain-of-thought, and telling Claude what to do instead of what to avoid. Each idea comes with a weak prompt and a rewritten strong prompt side by side, so you can copy the pattern rather than the wording.
who_for: Anyone whose Claude answers come out generic and who wants a short, ordered list of fixes to try today.
skip_if: Skip it if you already use examples, explicit constraints and chain-of-thought by habit - this stops at general craft and never gets into evals or model-specific tuning.

title: Steering Claude Code: when to use CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, and subagents
author: Anthropic
summary: Compares the seven ways you can give Claude Code standing instructions - root and nested CLAUDE.md, path-scoped rules, skills, subagents, hooks - and judges each one by two things: how much context window it eats and how hard it binds. The useful part is the decision rules, for example keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, put deploy and review procedures in a skill, use a path-scoped rule for a cross-cutting file constraint, and reach for a subagent when the side task would clutter the main thread.
who_for: Developers who already run Claude Code daily and now have a messy CLAUDE.md, or a team arguing about where project conventions should live.
skip_if: Skip it if you have not yet used Claude Code on a real project - it assumes you know what a session, a compaction and a slash command are, and teaches none of them.

title: Claude Code overview and install guide
author: Anthropic
summary: The front door of the Claude Code documentation. It gives the exact install command for every surface - terminal on macOS, Linux, Windows PowerShell and CMD, Homebrew, WinGet, VS Code, JetBrains, desktop app and browser - then shows what the tool is actually good at, with one-line example prompts for writing tests, fixing bugs, committing and opening pull requests. A short table at the end routes you to the right page for CI automation, scheduling, Slack and browser debugging.
who_for: A developer installing Claude Code for the first time who needs the correct command for their operating system and a map of what to read next.
skip_if: Skip it if Claude Code is already installed and working - it is an index page, so everything past the install block is links rather than instruction.

title: Best practices for Claude Code
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's internal working patterns, all built on one constraint: the context window fills fast and quality drops as it fills. It covers giving Claude a check it can run so it stops guessing when it is done, the explore-plan-implement-commit loop with plan mode, before-and-after prompt rewrites, what belongs in CLAUDE.md versus a skill or a hook, and how to scale out with non-interactive mode, parallel sessions and an adversarial review subagent. It ends with five named failure patterns and the fix for each.
who_for: Someone past the first week with Claude Code whose sessions keep drifting, and teams that want a shared house style for agentic coding.
skip_if: Skip it if you have never run a Claude Code session - the advice is corrective, so without your own bad habits to match against it reads as a list of abstractions.

title: Building effective agents
author: Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang, Anthropic
summary: The essay that gave the industry its vocabulary for agent design. It separates workflows (fixed code paths) from agents (the model directs itself), then walks five composable patterns - prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation by sectioning or voting, orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimiser - each with a diagram and a rule for when to reach for it. The closing appendix on prompt-engineering your tools is the part most people miss and the part most worth reading.
who_for: Developers about to build their first multi-step LLM system who want to know which pattern fits before they pick a framework.
skip_if: Skip it if you need current implementation detail: it is from December 2024, Anthropic has added a banner saying the tooling has changed, and it points you at Managed Agents instead.

title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
author: Barry Zhang, Keith Lazuka and Mahesh Murag, Anthropic
summary: Explains the design idea behind Agent Skills using the real PDF skill as the worked example. Three levels of progressive disclosure - name and description at startup, the SKILL.md body when the task matches, bundled files only when needed - are what let a skill carry unlimited context without filling the window. It also covers bundling scripts so Claude runs code instead of generating tokens, four authoring guidelines that start from evaluation, and a blunt warning that a malicious skill can exfiltrate your data.
who_for: Anyone writing their first SKILL.md who wants to understand why the format is shaped this way before copying a template.
skip_if: Skip it if you want step-by-step authoring instructions - this is the reasoning behind skills, and it hands the how-to off to the docs and the cookbook.

title: Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK
author: Anthropic
summary: The post that renamed the Claude Code SDK to the Claude Agent SDK and explains why: the same harness that gives Claude a terminal, a filesystem and search turns out to power finance, research, support and personal-assistant agents just as well as coding ones. It frames every agent as the loop gather context, take action, verify work, repeat, and walks that loop through a worked email-agent example.
who_for: Developers deciding whether to build an agent on the Agent SDK rather than wiring their own tool loop over the Messages API.
skip_if: Skip it if you want runnable code - it is a five-minute design argument with an illustrative example, not a tutorial with a repository to clone.

title: Claude Platform documentation home
author: Anthropic
summary: The developer entry point for building on Claude. It makes you pick a surface first - Messages, where you write every turn and your own tool loop, or Managed Agents, where Anthropic hosts stateful agent sessions for you - then lays the rest out as a four-stage lifecycle: get started, build (thinking, vision, tool use, structured outputs, prompt caching, streaming), evaluate and ship (evals, batch testing, guardrails, cost), and operate (workspaces, keys, usage, model migration). A hello-world snippet is shown in nine languages.
who_for: A developer with an API key who needs to find the right page fast, or someone comparing the direct API against managed agent hosting.
skip_if: Skip it if you work only in Claude Code or the Claude app - nothing here applies until you are writing API calls yourself.

title: Claude Cookbooks
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's own library of runnable Jupyter notebooks, organised by job rather than by feature: classification, retrieval-augmented generation, summarisation, tool use with a worked customer-service agent, vision and chart reading, PDF handling, JSON mode, moderation filters, prompt caching, automated evals and a cost-optimisation walkthrough that measures pass rate against cost per task. Newer folders cover the Agent SDK, managed agents, skills and observability.
who_for: Developers who learn by running and modifying working code, and anyone who needs a defensible starting point for a specific capability instead of a blank file.
skip_if: Skip it if you do not have an API key with credits - the notebooks call the paid API, and reading them without running them gives you far less than the time costs.

title: Anthropic courses: API fundamentals, prompting, evals and tool use
author: Anthropic
summary: Five notebook courses that Anthropic tells you to take in order: API fundamentals (keys, parameters, multimodal prompts, streaming), the long interactive prompt-engineering tutorial, real-world prompting for messy production prompts, writing prompt evaluations that actually measure quality, and tool use end to end. The prompt-engineering course also exists in AWS Workshop and Google Vertex versions.
who_for: A developer who wants one ordered path from first API call to evaluated, tool-using prompts, without paying for a course platform.
skip_if: Skip it if you want current model behaviour - the material deliberately uses Claude 3 Haiku to keep student API bills low, so the model choices and some SDK patterns are behind.

title: anthropics/skills: example Agent Skills and the skill spec
author: Anthropic
summary: The reference collection of real SKILL.md files, ranging from creative and design skills to MCP server generation and enterprise workflows, plus the Agent Skills specification and a blank template. The genuinely valuable part is the docx, pdf, pptx and xlsx folders: these are the production skills behind Claude's document features, published so you can see how a complex skill is actually structured. The README also shows the two-field frontmatter and the plugin-marketplace install commands.
who_for: Anyone writing a custom skill who wants to read good examples first, and Claude Code users who want the document skills installed as a plugin.
skip_if: Skip it if you want an explanation of why skills work the way they do - this is a folder of examples with a thin README, so read the Agent Skills engineering post first.

title: Claude for Product Management
author: Anthropic
summary: A short official demo video showing product teams using Claude with Artifacts and Projects, wrapped in a note about which plan each feature needs: Artifacts on every plan, Projects on Pro and Team or Enterprise, project sharing on Team or Enterprise only. The plan table is the durable part; the walkthrough itself is a demo rather than a lesson.
who_for: A product manager on a Team or Enterprise plan who wants to see the shape of a PM workflow in Claude before setting one up.
skip_if: Skip it if you want written steps or prompts you can copy - the page is almost entirely an embedded video with no transcript and no examples on the page.

title: Model Context Protocol: Advanced Topics
author: Anthropic Academy
summary: The second MCP course, aimed at people who already ship servers. It covers sampling (letting the server ask the client for a model call, which moves cost and complexity to the client), progress and logging notifications for long operations, roots-based directory permissions, the full JSON message taxonomy of requests versus notifications, the stdio handshake, StreamableHTTP with server-sent events and session management, and when to run stateless HTTP so you can scale horizontally behind a load balancer. Each concept has a code walkthrough lesson and there is an assessment at the end.
who_for: Developers taking an MCP server from a local demo to something deployed, who need to choose a transport and understand the trade-offs.
skip_if: Skip it if you have not built a basic MCP server yet - it assumes Python async, JSON-RPC and server-sent events, and never covers the basics.

title: AI Fluency for pK-12 Educators (learning path)
author: Anthropic Academy
summary: A two-course path built on the 4D framework of Delegation, Description, Discernment and Diligence. The first course is for a teacher's own practice; the second, Train the Trainer, hands you a ready-to-run workshop kit so you can lead the same session for colleagues. Both are pitched at teachers' professional values rather than at the tooling, and registration is free.
who_for: School teachers and anyone responsible for staff AI training in a pK-12 setting who needs material they can deliver, not just read.
skip_if: Skip it if you teach at university level or want Claude product training - the framing, examples and workshop kit are all built for pK-12 classrooms.

title: AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations
author: Anthropic Academy, with Rick Dakan and Joseph Feller
summary: Anthropic's own beginner course on Coursera, ten modules and about three hours, teaching the 4D framework: pick the right tasks to hand to AI, describe them clearly, judge the output with discernment, and apply diligence about responsible use. It is written to survive tool changes, so the skills carry across models rather than teaching Claude's buttons. Rated 4.7 from 105 reviews and refreshed in May 2026.
who_for: Someone who has typed a few prompts and got mediocre results, and wants a mental model for what to delegate before learning any specific product.
skip_if: Skip it if you want hands-on Claude practice - the course is deliberately tool-independent, so you finish with a framework rather than a working setup.

title: Claude Code: Software Engineering with Generative AI Agents
author: Dr. Jules White
summary: Six modules, about five hours, framed around orchestrating Claude Code the way a tech lead directs several senior engineers rather than the way you use autocomplete. It covers prompt patterns and context engineering, designing codebases and processes so an agent can work in them, rapid prototyping, and quality assurance on agent output. Beginner level with two graded assignments; rated 4.7 from 171 reviews with about 48,000 enrolled.
who_for: Developers who want a structured, assessed course on agentic coding rather than a pile of blog posts, and who like Jules White's prompt-pattern teaching style.
skip_if: Skip it if you want deep coverage of hooks, subagents and MCP internals - this is a beginner orchestration course, and Anthropic's own best-practices docs go further for free.

title: Next-Generation AI Assistant: Claude by Anthropic
author: Vinita Silaparasetty (Starweaver)
summary: A two-hour guided project that walks one thread end to end: set up an Anthropic account, name a digital product, write its description, build a promotional campaign and draft a launch plan, each step practising open and closed prompts tuned for audience, context, specificity and tone. Eight short videos plus one graded assessment.
who_for: A marketer or small-business owner who has used ChatGPT casually and wants a single guided exercise that ends with real campaign copy.
skip_if: Skip it if the title made you think Anthropic built it - it is a Coursera and Starweaver production, one module long, rated only 4.1 from 33 reviews, and it never leaves basic marketing prompts.

title: MCP: Build Rich-Context AI Apps with Anthropic
author: Elie Schoppik, Head of Technical Education at Anthropic
summary: Eleven video lessons and six code examples, just under two hours, taught by Anthropic's head of technical education. You build a research chatbot with custom tools, convert it into an MCP-compatible application, write a local server with FastMCP that exposes tools, resources and prompt templates, test it with MCP Inspector, add an MCP client inside the chatbot, connect to Anthropic's reference filesystem and fetch servers, wire it into Claude Desktop, and finally deploy the server remotely.
who_for: Python developers who want one guided pass through both sides of MCP - client and server - instead of assembling it from documentation.
skip_if: Skip it if you are new to Python or to LLM app development, and note it was recorded in May 2025, so the Python SDK has since moved to v2 and some code needs adjusting.

title: Claude Cowork Tutorial: How to Use Anthropic's AI Desktop Agent
author: Bex Tuychiev
summary: An honest hands-on report rather than a feature tour. The author points Cowork at a 186-file Downloads folder and shows the exact prompt and the result, then batch-converts and compresses documents, then turns a finance-app backup into a ten-page PDF spending report. A comparison table separates Claude chat, Cowork and Claude Code by filesystem access and by what each one actually does. The last third is the useful part: the xlsx skill breaks on presentation-style spreadsheets, and Chrome automation works but took over thirty minutes for three unsubscribes because every step is a screenshot round trip.
who_for: Non-coders deciding whether Cowork is worth switching to, who want to see failure modes as well as demos.
skip_if: Skip it if you already use Cowork daily - the examples are entry level and the advanced sections stop at naming skills, connectors and scheduling rather than teaching them.

title: How to Build an MCP Server with Python, Docker, and Claude Code
author: Balajee Asish Brahmandam
summary: Builds a working project-scaffolder MCP server in about a hundred lines of FastMCP, containerises it in a six-line Dockerfile, and registers it with one claude mcp add command - all from the terminal, no desktop app. It calls out the two bugs that break most first attempts: anything printed to stdout corrupts the JSON-RPC stream, and Docker needs PYTHONUNBUFFERED plus the -i flag. A long security section covers the GitHub MCP prompt-injection incident, two named CVEs, path-traversal validation and least-privilege tokens, which almost no other MCP tutorial does.
who_for: Developers who want a deployable MCP server they can hand to someone else, and anyone who needs the security argument written down.
skip_if: Skip it if you do not have Docker and a Claude Code subscription ready, or if you only want the concept - this is a build-along and reading it without typing gains you little.

title: Claude Code Essentials (ExamPro full course)
author: Andrew Brown (ExamPro), posted by Beau Carnes
summary: A free full-length video course with an unusually complete CLI syllabus. Beyond the agentic loop and the explore-plan-code pattern, it grinds through the operational detail most tutorials skip: install on PowerShell, CMD, Linux and VS Code, the doctor command, auth tokens and usage limits, resume and fork of sessions, compact, clear, rename and rewind, ccusage and cost commands, third-party providers including Bedrock, Foundry and Vertex, status line and session data, and permission rules for Bash, MCP and WebFetch.
who_for: Developers who want one long guided video covering the whole Claude Code surface, including billing and permissions, without paying for a course.
skip_if: Skip it if you learn badly from long video - the same ground is covered faster in Anthropic's written docs, and a video course dates quickly as CLI commands change.

title: The Claude Code Handbook
author: Vahe Aslanyan
summary: A twenty-five chapter free handbook that runs from installation and subscription costs through prompt discipline, plan mode, feature-by-feature building, context and session management, MCP integrations, subagents and parallel workflows, skills and persistent rules, autonomous loops, and code review and verification, ending with starter project blueprints and a structured path forward. It is unusually clear-eyed with non-technical readers: it states plainly that Claude Code removes the coding barrier and none of the others, so you still own the problem, the users and the distribution.
who_for: Someone who wants one long, ordered document instead of thirty tabs, including founders and domain experts with no programming background.
skip_if: Skip it if you are already fluent with Claude Code - the first eight chapters are background on Anthropic and the model family, and the depth per topic is lower than the official docs.

title: Claude Code for Product Managers
author: Marcus Moretti
summary: A general manager running a whole product alone describes what is left of product management once Claude Code absorbs the busywork. He writes only the roadmap by hand; every PRD and ticket is generated, GitHub issues replace a separate tracker, and the work collapses from ten apps into one thread. The accompanying compound-engineering plugin, including a strategy skill that interviews you to produce the roadmap document, is open source and free even though the essay is not.
who_for: Solo or near-solo product owners who want a concrete account of a working end-to-end Claude Code PM setup, plus a plugin to copy.
skip_if: Skip it if you will not subscribe to Every - the free portion stops at the roadmap section, and the three most specific claims sit behind the paywall.

title: How to use Claude Code for non-engineering use cases
author: Rich Holmes
summary: Written on the assumption that you have never opened a terminal. The free opening covers what Claude Code is, the native install command for Mac and Windows, first login, and setting up an IDE purely as a file browser rather than an editor. The paid remainder promises downloadable agent templates for PRD and Jira ticket writing, spreadsheet and local file editing, SEO audits, a markdown second brain, and examples of product managers and designers assembling a Product OS.
who_for: Product managers and designers who want the setup explained without assuming terminal familiarity, and who want ready-made agent templates.
skip_if: Skip it unless you will pay for the newsletter - the free part ends exactly where the templates begin, and it is from December 2025 so some install and IDE detail has moved on.

title: Everyone should be using Claude Code more
author: Lenny Rachitsky
summary: The piece that reframed Claude Code for people who do not write code: stop reading the word Code and think Claude Local or Claude Agent, an intelligent process running on your own machine that can handle far bigger files and far longer tasks than a browser chat. It then collects fifty concrete uses gathered from readers and the author - organising folders, cleaning up images, summarising customer calls, creating Linear tickets, and so on.
who_for: Non-technical professionals who keep hearing about Claude Code and need a persuasive, example-heavy reason to install it.
skip_if: Skip it if you want method rather than inspiration - it is a list of what other people do, most of it sits behind a paid subscription, and it dates from October 2025 so it predates Cowork.

title: How I AI: Claude Code for product managers, with Teresa Torres
author: Claire Vo, with Teresa Torres
summary: A screen-sharing episode where the author of Continuous Discovery Habits shows the personal system she built in Claude Code: a markdown task manager that replaced Trello because she wanted control and searchability, an automated daily digest of relevant academic papers, a deliberate structure for context files so Claude gets what it needs without drowning, and slash commands that remove daily friction. She also talks about keeping her own voice while writing with Claude.
who_for: Product people and researchers who want to watch a non-developer's real terminal setup rather than read about one, especially for research collection and writing.
skip_if: Skip it if you want copyable configuration - it is a demonstration and conversation, so you get the shape of the system and have to rebuild the files yourself.

title: How to Use Claude Code: Complete Tutorial for Product Managers
author: Aakash Gupta, with Carl Vellotti
summary: A long interview published with a full timestamped transcript on the page, so you can read it instead of listening. Carl Vellotti walks a beginner path from why a non-technical person should leave the chat interface at all, through research and writing use cases, prototyping, and finally building small agents that coordinate recurring work. The transcript format makes it easy to jump to the section you need.
who_for: Product managers who prefer a conversational explanation with a searchable transcript, and who want the argument for leaving the chat window.
skip_if: Skip it if you want precise, current instructions - it is a conversation with no publication date shown on the page, so treat the version-specific detail as unverified.

title: Getting started with Claude Cowork (Airtree course)
author: Marnix Denys, Airtree
summary: A venture firm built this one-hour course to get its own non-technical staff using Cowork, then published it. It is deliberately internal in tone: a setup guide including which subscription you need, then task-shaped exercises drawn from work people had been doing manually for years. Downloadable, no registration, and it tells you to ask the AI itself when you get stuck.
who_for: Teams that need a short, ready-made onboarding session for non-technical colleagues rather than a self-study reading list.
skip_if: Skip it if you already automate work with Cowork or Claude Code - it is beginner material by design and stops at the one-hour mark.

title: Complete Guide to Claude Cowork (Claude Code for Everyone)
author: Carl Vellotti
summary: A free guide designed to be worked through inside Cowork itself. It teaches a Done framework - decide what finished looks like, what context Claude needs, and which constraints matter - then gives prompt templates for file organisation, research synthesis, document creation and data extraction, a recommended folder structure, and a section on sub-agents. It sits inside a larger free site that also has role-specific pages for writers, marketers, researchers, analysts and founders.
who_for: Non-developers who want prompt templates and a folder setup they can copy today, and people who like learning a tool by using it.
skip_if: Skip it if you want an independent assessment of limits - it is a teaching site written by an enthusiast, so pair it with a review that documents what Cowork does badly.

title: Build Your PM Operating System on Claude Code
author: Ron Yang
summary: A two-week live cohort where you build a persistent context layer for your own product - company, product, personas, competitors - so Claude stops needing re-briefing every session. You then run pre-built skills for PRDs, roadmaps and competitive analysis, chain them into discovery-to-delivery workflows, and set up six review subagents (CTO, UX lead, sales, executive, user advocate, devil's advocate) to pressure-test your artefacts before your colleagues do. Taught by a former Aha! VP of product; rated 4.6 from 13 reviews.
who_for: Solo or overloaded product managers who already use AI ad hoc and want a repeatable system, built on their own product during the course.
skip_if: Skip it if you cannot commit to live sessions or will not pay - it needs a Claude Code Pro or Max subscription on top of the course fee, and 13 reviews is a weak quality signal.

title: Craft a Professional AI Developer Setup (Cursor & Claude Code)
author: Steve Kinney
summary: Twenty-five lessons, about 3.7 hours, on assembling a professional agentic workflow rather than on any single tool. It covers inline edits versus agent mode, writing markdown project plans with guardrails and linting so output stays on track, delegating long tasks to Claude Code on a branch in the background, adding MCP servers for external services, and managing the context window with project boundaries and compaction. Rated 4.6.
who_for: Working front-end and full-stack developers who want an opinionated setup covering both Cursor and Claude Code from someone who ships with them.
skip_if: Skip it if you only want Claude Code - roughly half the course is Cursor - and note it was published in August 2025, so parts of both tools have changed since recording.

title: MCP Python SDK
author: Model Context Protocol maintainers
summary: The official Python implementation of MCP and the fastest way to expose your own data and tools to Claude. The repository is now on v2, a substantial rework that supports the current spec revision and fixes long-standing architecture problems; the README links a get-started guide, a what-is-new tour and a full migration guide, and it warns that pip install mcp now pulls 2.x, so pin below 2 until you migrate. The v1.x branch still receives security fixes.
who_for: Python developers writing an MCP server or client, and anyone maintaining an older MCP integration that suddenly broke.
skip_if: Skip it if you want to learn what MCP is - the README assumes that and sends you to the documentation site, so start with a course or the freeCodeCamp build-along instead.

title: MCP reference servers
author: Model Context Protocol maintainers
summary: A small, deliberately curated set of reference server implementations - Everything, Fetch and a handful of others - maintained by the MCP steering group and stated outright to be educational examples rather than production software. Reading one end to end is the quickest way to see how tools, resources and prompts are declared in practice. It also indexes the official SDKs for ten languages and points to the MCP Registry if you are hunting for servers to use rather than to study.
who_for: Developers who learn a protocol by reading a small correct implementation before writing their own.
skip_if: Skip it if you want servers to deploy - the maintainers warn these are demonstrations without production security hardening, and the registry is the right place for real ones.

title: A Guide to Claude Code 2.0 and getting better at using coding agents
author: sankalp
summary: A long practitioner write-up from someone who switched away from Claude Code and came back. It goes past feature lists into how things behave: whether subagents inherit context and how they are spawned, why agents are token guzzlers and what context engineering actually means in a session, running MCP servers with code execution, what the system-reminder blocks in Claude's prompts are, and how hooks, skills and reminders combine. There is a separate section written for readers who are not deeply technical.
who_for: Developers who already use Claude Code and want mechanism-level understanding of subagents and context, told through one person's tested workflow.
skip_if: Skip it if you need current detail - it documents Claude Code 2.0 as of December 2025, and both the CLI and the model line-up have moved on since.

title: Claude for K-12 Teachers: context steering, Projects and Skills
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: A teacher's argument against the lesson-plan-in-one-prompt habit, followed by a repeatable setup: put your teaching context in a steering.md file, attach it to a Claude Project, add small specialist files for things like grammar requirements or class neurodiversity adaptations, work out a process in ordinary conversation, test it on lessons you actually teach, and only then freeze it into a Skill. The worked example is a process-based student portfolio that collects evidence during an assignment rather than judging the final artefact.
who_for: School teachers with free educator access who want a durable setup instead of one-off prompts, and who are curious about writing their own skills.
skip_if: Skip it if you teach at university or need assessment-policy guidance - this is classroom practice for K-12 and says nothing about institutional rules.

title: Building a Claude Project for Teaching & Learning (recording)
author: Northeastern University, AI in Teaching & Learning
summary: A recorded university session on designing a Claude Project that acts as a course assistant - what to load into project knowledge, how to write the project instructions, and how students then interact with it. The page bundles the recording with a downloadable handout and a faculty FAQ about AI in teaching, so you get the workshop materials rather than only the video.
who_for: University instructors who want to see a colleague build a course-specific Claude Project before making one for their own module.
skip_if: Skip it if you need current interface detail - the recording is labelled 2025, so the Projects screens and features shown are behind what you will see today.
